public_rationale: Combined interpretation performed best in the knee MRI experiment. However, the contemporaneous radiologist experiment found that assistance did not uniformly improve diagnosis and sometimes performed worse than AI alone. The evidence supports collaboration in some settings, but not a general claim that it consistently delivers the best diagnostic results.
limitations: Results depend on the task, readers and collaboration workflow.
The studies have different designs and do not support a pooled numerical estimate.
A narrower claim that some well-designed combinations perform best would receive a more favorable assessment.

criteria.support_condition: Comparative studies show that combined human–AI interpretation generally achieves better diagnostic performance than either component alone.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Comparative studies show that combined interpretation does not generally outperform the better component. Substantial differences between tasks or workflows warrant a mixed assessment.

evidence.explanation: This radiologist experiment found that AI assistance did not uniformly improve diagnostic quality; its performance analysis also identified ranges where AI alone exceeded assisted radiologists. The delegation conclusion additionally accounts for reading time, so it is not a pure accuracy ranking.
